Caring for a new baby is a big responsibility any time, but a first baby during a time like this could be even more anxiety provoking. I agree with all the suggestions of companionship, presence of a wise and calm older woman whom she trusts, and lots of support from you. I am not a fan of Xanax because I saw how my father struggled with it. He was depression prone, and he reached for it when he was feeling anxious. He used pills rather than develop better coping skills, and after a heart attack, he developed a heavy Xanax habit. It took a couple of years to get him back off those pills, in part because doctors would so willingly re-up his prescriptions. Meantime, those who lived with him saw his personality change for the worse and dealt with his nightmares and delusions. It can be wicked stuff and doesn't really resolve anything.

 

Although I didn't have PPD, I struggle with the same familial depression as my father did. What I have found helpful over the years is to find something productive on which I can focus. With babies, there are a great many books, articles, and other resources to tell you how to care for them. Back in my time, it was baby magazines, which usually were given as a gift subscription by some helpful relative. All this advice is good to a point, but it can also provoke anxiety because it can be conflicting, and it can lead to feelings of never getting it right. I felt like I turned a corner as a new mom when I cancelled the subscriptions and stopped reading most of the advice. Unless I had a specific question, it just wasn't really helpful. It's like one day I woke up and realized that what I had at home wasn't a generic 'baby', but a living, breathing, unique human being who had blessed our family with his presence. I set about tuning into him, his moods, his personality. When I stopped thinking of him as 'a baby' and stopped obsessing on his milestones and the enormity of it all, I felt better and became a calmer, better mom. Each child is different, and will grow and develop in his or her own way. Unless there is something drastically wrong, it will unfold with gentle daily tending. Hungry babies eat, tired babies sleep, and although they can be cranky and not do it on our schedules, generally they settle into a pattern. Anxious parenting can interfere with that process. Forcing babies to eat when we think they should doesn't work too well. There is a time and place for setting schedules and discipline for children, but little babies need a period of time during which we totally tune in to them. They aren't great communicators yet, so it's on us to read their clumsy signals. Time spent just holding, loving, and learning to understand this new little person may calm her. If the weather is nice where you live, go outside and put your baby down on a blanket and enjoy the sunshine together. Listen to the birds and smells of nature. Keep it simple. Babies don't need all the stuff that people are promoting. Babies need parental love, holding, food, and just enough cleanliness to be safe. Encourage her a lot and build her confidence. We have over-intellectualized this among humans but our instincts for parenting are still present below the surface. Some of her anxiety is hormonal, some is situational, and some is the enormity of her love for this baby. It's easier to say than to do, but focusing that enormous love on building the emotional ties within her family rather than focusing on her own insecurities is a positive path forward.

 

As a last thought, consider her friendships and social media activities. There can be peer pressure regarding 'perfect parenting' or an unhealthy focus on milestones among moms. Some people thrive on that sort of community while others come out of it feeling inadequate and anxious. Some of us do better with a time of privacy when there are changes in the family.
